the role of the neuroendocrine cells of prostate cancer in androgen-independent tumor progression.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of neuroendocrine cells in prostate cancer, and how these cells may contribute to the progression of prostate cancer.
the role of neuroendocrine (NE) cells in prostate cancer.

the PKA pathway is an important regulator of prostate cancer cell proliferation and survival.

neuroendocrine cells are not the cause of androgen-independent prostate cancer, but rather they are a consequence of androgen-independent growth and are a contributing factor in the progression of this disease.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neuroendocrine cells in prostate tumors may contribute to tumor growth by providing growth signals to the surrounding cells.

PKA-differentiation of prostate cancer cells can be used to model neuroendocrine differentiation and to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying the paracrine growth stimulation of prostate cancer cells by neuroendocrine cells.
the PKA signaling pathway is a potential target for the treatment of prostate cancer, particularly in the androgen-independent setting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prostate cancer cells can be stimulated to grow in a paracrinic fashion by the presence of caPKA-expressing neuroendocrine cells, even under conditions of androgendependent growth.
neuroendocrine cells in the prostate can enhance the growth of prostate cancer cells, and this effect is particularly pronounced when the cancer is androgen-independent.
neuroendocrine cells are not just bystanders in the prostate, and in fact they may be contributing to the progression of the disease.
